messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Anjali Mehta is a 47-year-old South Asian American pastor who came to treatment after months of telling her congregation that she was “just tired” and then finding that even the ordinary rituals of ministry had become hard to bear. During a period overseas doing church-related humanitarian work, she was detained, interrogated, and tortured. What stays with her are not a complete set of memories so much as sharp, unbearable fragments: the taste forced into her mouth, the sound of herself crying, the pressure of having to answer questions while trying to speak. Some moments are searingly clear and others vanish entirely. She can describe one instant with painful precision and then reaches a blank space she cannot cross, and when those pieces return she is flooded with guilt, as if she should have endured differently or protected someone by saying less or more.

Since returning home, the triggers are woven into the life she is trying to resume. In pastoral visits and after Sunday services, church members often press food on her, and a particular taste can stop her cold before she has formed any thought about why. Her body lurches into alarm first; she feels the danger in her throat, stomach, and chest before her mind catches up. Crying—especially when she hears someone sob during prayer—or simply being asked to talk about what happened can pull up disconnected pieces of the detention, a few images suddenly vivid while the rest remains missing. Those broken recollections leave her feeling intensely guilty and more convinced that she cannot handle what is in her own mind.

Because she has come to believe that if she lets herself think about the torture she will be overwhelmed, Anjali works hard to keep it out of awareness. She suppresses thoughts, cuts off conversations that move too close to the subject, and has become rigid about food, telling herself that strict control over eating is the only way to stay steady. At church potlucks and in parishioners’ homes, she avoids unfamiliar dishes and often claims she has already eaten. The more frightened she becomes by the idea of losing control internally, the more tightly she tries to manage what she consumes and what she allows herself to remember. She has also grown markedly watchful around people, scanning faces, tone of voice, and small shifts in posture for signs of threat, as if danger might be concealed behind friendliness. Because she kept cutting short conversations, refusing food, and steering herself away from anything that might test her fear, she never remained in those moments long enough to learn that they could pass without catastrophe, and the danger therefore continued to feel immediate and real.

These efforts have not brought relief. Pushing the memories away seems to leave them more disjointed, so that what returns does so in abrupt pieces rather than a story she can place in the past. After one of those jagged fragments surfaced, the rest of the day often became newly hazardous to her; the sound of someone crying down the hall, a question asked too directly, even the taste of a familiar dish could seem charged with the unfinished memory and seize her before she could orient herself. That fragmentation itself deepens her despair. When she cannot make the memory cohere, she takes it as evidence that something in her has been permanently damaged, and she has begun to say, quietly and with shame, that she is no longer capable of doing the work that once defined her. With that conviction in place, she moves through church life expecting herself to be thrown off balance, and cues she once would have absorbed without notice now catch hard: a parishioner’s tears, a direct question, or food pressed into her hands feels immediately loaded because she assumes she cannot trust her own mind to stay steady. Once she had come to see herself as damaged and unable to trust her own mind, ordinary ambiguities stopped feeling ordinary; a parishioner’s tears, an unexpected question, or food offered after worship more readily registered as signs that she was about to lose control again. She used to be the person others leaned on in crisis; now she worries she has no future beyond enduring the next day without breaking apart.

Her sense of present danger has thickened over time. Because the memories arrive as disconnected flashes and her body reacts before she can think, reassurance from others does not reach her. Colleagues tell her she is safe in her church office, yet she remains superalert, listening for footsteps in the hallway and watching who enters the sanctuary. This constant on-guard feeling feeds her conviction that safety cannot be trusted anywhere, which in turn makes ordinary cues more potent. A parishioner crying in her office, a well-meant question about her time abroad, even the prospect of communion elements or shared meals can feel charged before anything has happened, and she braces herself as though the past is about to recur.

That fear has started to alter her ministry in concrete ways. She delegates pastoral counseling when she expects tears, shortens visits that might lead to personal disclosure, and avoids communal meals after services. She tells herself these are sensible limits, but privately she hears them as proof that she is failing in her calling. The more she reads her retreat from others as evidence that she is diminished, the more hopeless she feels; the more hopeless she feels, the less able she is to risk remembering, speaking, or eating freely. By the time she sought help, she was dreading Sunday mornings, not because she no longer cared about her congregation, but because every part of the role exposed her to crying, questions, food, and people she could not stop scanning. What finally brought her in was the fear that if this continued, she would have to leave the ministry entirely. What she wants, though she says it cautiously, is to believe that her life is not over and that she might someday stand at the altar, hear another person weep, and remain fully present instead of disappearing into terror.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette describes triggers evoking alarm and memories, but does not clearly state within one paragraph that triggers lead Anjali to use avoidance or other maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: Although negative appraisals make cues feel more loaded, the vignette does not clearly convey in one paragraph that her negative beliefs cause triggers themselves to arise or become triggering stimuli.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: Threat is described as making ordinary cues more potent, but there is no clear same-paragraph statement that her sense of threat leads directly to negative appraisals or distorted beliefs.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows avoidance maintaining threat and fragmented memory, but does not clearly state within one paragraph that maladaptive strategies lead to stronger negative appraisals about herself or her situation.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Since returning home, the triggers are woven into the life she is trying to resume. In pastoral visits and after Sunday services, church members often press food on her, and a particular taste can stop her cold before she has formed any thought about why.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
After moments like that, Anjali becomes immediately strategic: she leaves receptions early, keeps water or mints with her to override any lingering taste, and avoids parishioners' kitchens whenever she can, because once a cue has caught hold of her she is certain the safest option is to get away before the rest of the reaction builds.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
That fragmentation itself deepens her despair. When she cannot make the memory cohere, she takes it as evidence that something in her has been permanently damaged, and she has begun to say, quietly and with shame, that she is no longer capable of doing the work that once defined her.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Having come to see herself as damaged and unreliable, she moves through ordinary church life expecting to be thrown off balance, and that expectation makes cues she once would have absorbed without notice—a parishioner's tears, a direct question, food pressed into her hands—stand out immediately as things that could undo her.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Her sense of present danger has thickened over time. Because the memories arrive as disconnected flashes and her body reacts before she can think, reassurance from others does not reach her.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Feeling this endangered so often has become, in her own mind, its own kind of proof: if her body will not let down its guard even in her church office, then she takes that as evidence that safety is no longer meant for her and that something in her has been fundamentally altered.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
That fear has started to alter her ministry in concrete ways. She delegates pastoral counseling when she expects tears, shortens visits that might lead to personal disclosure, and avoids communal meals after services.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each time she has to arrange her day around these precautions, it lands on her as further evidence that she cannot cope in the way she once could; the very fact that she still needs all this managing confirms, to her, that she is diminished and no longer trustworthy in her role.
<<<END>>>
